50 Boutique Wine Importers and Distributors in the USA
29/10/2026 From specialists in natural wines and family estates to regional wholesalers serving independent retailers, these are companies wineries should know when building their U.S. distribution strategy.
For a boutique winery, the right U.S. partner does more than arrange the movement of bottles. It understands the producer, identifies suitable accounts, and gives its sales team a clear reason to recommend the wine.
That makes portfolio fit essential. A specialist in Italian family estates may be well suited to an unfamiliar indigenous variety. A natural-wine importer may place particular importance on farming and cellar practices. A regional distributor may offer the focused market coverage a small winery can realistically support.
The following guide brings together 50 boutique and specialist wine importers and distributors serving the United States. Some are small businesses with tightly focused portfolios; others are larger companies that maintain a strong commitment to independent producers.
Official websites and company portfolio information were checked for this article on October 28, 2026. This is an editorial guide, not a sales ranking. Importing and wholesale distribution are different services, and inclusion does not mean a company is currently accepting new producers.
Importers With a Strong Grower and Estate Focus
1. Kermit Lynch Wine Merchant
Kermit Lynch Wine Merchant imports wines from France and Italy, with a portfolio spanning celebrated regions and less familiar appellations. Its producer-centered approach makes it an important reference for wineries studying specialist importing. Producers should examine the existing growers and regional coverage before proposing a fit.
2. Rosenthal Wine Merchant
Rosenthal Wine Merchant emphasizes small, family-owned estates and wines that communicate their origins. Its portfolio includes producers from France, Italy, Switzerland, Spain, and Austria. For wineries, the central question is whether their vineyards, winemaking, and regional identity complement the merchant’s established approach.
3. Louis/Dressner Selections
Louis/Dressner Selections has longstanding relationships with independent growers and a strong interest in farming and winemaking practices. Its website provides extensive producer information and harvest reports. Wineries researching the business should be ready to discuss their work in the vineyard and cellar in detail.
4. Skurnik Wines & Spirits
Skurnik Wines & Spirits combines national importing with direct wholesale distribution in selected states. Its portfolio includes boutique producers from around the world. Suppliers should distinguish between a national import relationship and a proposal for a specific wholesale market, then approach the relevant team accordingly.
5. T. Edward Wines & Spirits
T. Edward Wines & Spirits began with boutique estates and continues to emphasize family-owned producers, craftsmanship, and authenticity. Its business includes importing and distribution. A winery’s introduction should explain the people behind the wine, its production philosophy, and its commercial role within the portfolio.
6. Bowler Wine
Bowler Wine is a New York-based importer and distributor focused on naturally made, small-production wines. Its selection emphasizes personality, regional character, and family growers. Wineries should research both its direct producer relationships and the other import portfolios it represents before making an introduction. NYC Wine Spirits Importer Distributor
7. European Cellars
European Cellars imports wines from family-owned properties practicing responsible viticulture. Its roots in France and Spain have expanded into other origins. Producers should assess how their wines express place and whether they add a distinct regional or stylistic contribution to the existing selection.
8. De Maison Selections
De Maison Selections is a national importer with a strong commitment to artisanal properties, regional heritage, and producer independence. Its business distinguishes national importing from direct distribution through De Maison East. Wineries should establish which relationship they are seeking before presenting their portfolio.
9. Polaner Selections
Polaner Selections combines established reference-point producers with smaller wineries, indigenous varieties, and less familiar regions. Its selection includes traditional producers and growers using organic or biodynamic practices. A compelling proposal should explain both the wine’s individuality and its value at the intended selling price.
10. Martine’s Wines
Martine’s Wines operates as an importer and wholesaler, with producer profiles and current wine information on its website. Its portfolio includes wines from established French regions and distinctive estates such as Domaine des Ardoisières. Suppliers should study the relevant regional selection before proposing additional representation. Importer & Wholesaler since 1979
Natural Wine and Small-Production Specialists
11. Jenny & François Selections
Jenny & François Selections focuses on natural wines from small growers. Its philosophy considers both vineyard practices and cellar methods. Producers researching the company should prepare a transparent account of farming, fermentation, additions, and production, alongside the practical information needed to evaluate a U.S. launch.
12. Zev Rovine Selections
Zev Rovine Selections works with growers who farm organically or biodynamically and favor minimal intervention in the cellar. Its producer list spans numerous countries. Wineries should assess philosophical fit and regional overlap, rather than assume a natural-wine identity alone creates an opening in the portfolio.
13. Selection Massale
Selection Massale imports natural wines from small wineries, emphasizing precision and drinkability. Its stated approach favors naturally fermented wines and growers working largely organically or biodynamically. Producers should explain how their practices translate into the wine’s character and consistency.
14. José Pastor Selections
José Pastor Selections champions small growers and traditionally made wines, with deep Spanish roots and a portfolio extending to other origins. Its selection includes regional grapes and distinctive vineyard environments. Wineries should explain what makes their wines an authentic expression of their particular place.
15. SelectioNaturel
SelectioNaturel specializes in Italian wines made in small quantities using natural and traditional methods. Its narrow focus makes regional and philosophical alignment especially important. Italian producers should study the represented growers and explain what their wines contribute beyond an appealing production story.
16. Vom Boden
Vom Boden focuses on small estates and growers whose work or locations sit outside the obvious mainstream. Its website includes current material on German wine. Producers considering the company should research its selection carefully and explain the vineyard, regional, and stylistic reasons their wines belong in that conversation.
17. Schatzi Wines
Schatzi Wines emphasizes the connection between growers and wine drinkers, with authenticity, sustainability, and terroir central to its approach. Its portfolio is built around producer relationships. Wineries should prepare clear information about their farming, wines, and expectations for a long-term importing partnership.
18. Olmstead Wine Co.
Olmstead Wine Co. is a Massachusetts distributor explicitly focused on natural wine. It provides a regional prospect for producers and importers whose wines fit that category. Suppliers should examine the portfolio and establish the current route for introducing new wines to the team.
19. Walden Selections
Walden Selections is a Washington State importer and distributor of wine and other beverages. It also appears in SelectioNaturel’s distribution network. Producers researching Washington should review the existing selection and discuss the specific importing or wholesale services required.
20. Nomadic Distribution
Nomadic Distribution presents itself as an importer and distributor of organic and natural wines. Its website includes producer information and a natural-wine shop. Suppliers should begin by reviewing the current producer list and confirming the relevant markets, portfolio needs, and submission process.
Regional and Country Specialists
21. The Piedmont Guy
The Piedmont Guy is a U.S.-based importer specializing in family-owned wineries from Piedmont. Its focused portfolio makes it particularly relevant to producers from that region. A pitch should explain the winery’s local identity, varieties, and position alongside the estates already represented.
22. Oliver McCrum Wines & Spirits
Oliver McCrum Wines & Spirits imports small-production Italian wines and operates distribution activities. Its stated preferences include clarity, freshness, indigenous varieties, and transparent winemaking. Producers should connect those characteristics with pricing and an account proposition that a sales team can readily explain.
23. Dalla Terra Italian Wine & Spirits
Dalla Terra describes its business as a national agent and direct importer for a select group of artisan, family-owned Italian wineries and spirits producers. Italian suppliers should understand its direct-import model and assess the existing regional portfolio before approaching the company.
24. Indigenous Selections
Indigenous Selections represents a curated group of Italian wineries selected for authenticity and regional character. Its portfolio covers origins including Piedmont, Tuscany, Veneto, Campania, Sicily, and Friuli. Producers should show how their wines offer a distinctive expression within the relevant region and price segment.
25. Porto Vino
Porto Vino maintains a French and Italian portfolio that includes producers from regions such as the Loire, Burgundy, Piedmont, and Sicily. Its website provides a detailed producer list. Suppliers should examine that regional coverage and explain where their wines add a meaningful point of difference.
26. North Berkeley Imports
North Berkeley Imports sources wines from France and Italy, combining importing with selected direct-market portfolios and distribution partners. Its offer reaches restaurants, wine shops, and collectors. Producers should distinguish the national portfolio opportunity from the company’s specific wholesale-market activities.
27. Michael Corso Selections
Michael Corso Selections is a specialist importer with a strong French wine focus. Its portfolio includes regions such as Alsace, Burgundy, the Loire, and the Rhône. Producers should present their regional credentials alongside a clear explanation of value and likely U.S. positioning.
28. Charles Neal Selections
Charles Neal Selections is a San Francisco-based importer and distributor with French wines and a substantial spirits selection. Its specialist approach makes it relevant to producers with a clear regional identity. Suppliers should explain the wine’s quality and commercial relevance without relying on small production as the sole selling point.
29. Brazos Wine Imports
Brazos Wine Imports focuses on artisan wines from Argentina, Chile, and Uruguay. Its stated interests include estate-grown, small-production wines that express specific places. South American producers should prepare detailed vineyard information and explain how the wines differ from more familiar market offerings.
30. Little Peacock Imports
Little Peacock Imports emphasizes a curated selection of family wineries, with producer listings covering Australia, France, Italy, and New Zealand. Its positioning combines discovery with commercial performance. Suppliers should explain why the wine is distinctive and how it can earn repeat purchases.
Curated Importers With Broader Portfolios
31. Grand Cru Selections
Grand Cru Selections is a New York-based importer and distributor with a strong fine-wine portfolio. Its producer information covers Champagne, Burgundy, and other regions. Wineries should research the existing estates closely and present a precise case for stylistic, regional, and commercial fit.
32. Coeur Wine Co.
Coeur Wine Co. emphasizes long-term producer relationships and wines it considers honest and authentic. Its website provides producer information and distribution partners. Suppliers should focus their introduction on the wine’s quality, its intended customer, and the practical foundations of a lasting relationship.
33. Communal Brands
Communal Brands combines production, importing, and distribution, with an emphasis on environmentally conscious wines and contemporary presentation. Its offer includes alternative formats such as boxed wine. Wineries should consider how product format, quality, and customer occasion work together within this business model.
34. Vine Connections
Vine Connections imports and distributes wines from family producers in origins including Argentina, Chile, Italy, France, and California. Its website provides trade tools such as technical sheets and shelf talkers. Producers should prepare a similarly complete set of materials when seeking representation. Global Wine, Sake & Spirits Importer
35. Massanois
Massanois is a national importer with direct distribution in selected markets. Its portfolio emphasizes quality-driven, family-owned wineries and distilleries. Suppliers should determine whether they need importing, direct wholesale distribution, or both, then tailor the proposal to the appropriate operation.
36. Banville Wine Merchants
Banville Wine Merchants combines national importing with wholesale operations in selected U.S. markets. Its approach centers on a selective, quality-focused portfolio. Producers should distinguish the national import opportunity from local distribution and identify the specific customer and price tier their wines would serve.
37. Regal Wine Imports
Regal Wine Imports maintains importing and distribution activities across wine and other beverage categories. Its website includes producer portfolios, trade information, and recent company content. Wineries should examine the relevant portfolio and market operation before proposing a new regional or stylistic addition.
38. Artisans & Vines
Artisans & Vines sources wines from Europe and several New World origins, emphasizing terroir and value. Its business includes importing, marketing, and distribution relationships. Suppliers should clarify the proposed territory and responsibilities, then connect their wine’s identity with a realistic market-development plan.
39. Wine Traditions
Wine Traditions seeks independent growers whose wines express their vineyards and offer accessible value. It operates as a national imp

Description:
Kim Engle and Debra Bermingham of Bloomer Creek began purchasing land and planting grapes in the early 1980's, eventually establishing their estate Bloomer Creek Vineyard in 1999 from 10 acres with two different vineyard designations - Auten Vineyard and Morehouse Road - planted on the west side of Cayuga Lake. In 2012, Barrow Vineyard was added to Bloomer Creek when Kim and Debra purchased an abandoned vineyard site on the east side of Seneca Lake, one mile from their production cellar in Hector, NY.
The 'Bloomers' meticulously farm their sites using organic methods - employing no herbicides or irrigation in the vineyard. The fruit is hand-harvested, and only native yeasts are used for fermentation, often utilizing whole clusters, extended lees aging, and allowing fermentations to progress at their own rate without using temperature control.
Bloomer Creek has always carved their own path and the results are wonderful. Their wines are incredibly distinctive, age-worthy and expressive of the place and time in which they were produced. That place is the Finger Lakes, and Bloomer Creek may be the single most unique, and compelling voice in town.

Description:
Bodegas Moraza is in San Vicente de la Sonsierra, one of the first villages in Rioja Alta to be known exclusively for the high quality of the wines made within its medieval settings. The village name means literally under the mountains, and indeed everywhere you look the towering mountains of Tolono - a part of the Sierra Cantabria - dominate the horizon. The small town stands left of the Ebro, the river that crosses the vast Rioja region, and it is here, surrounded by vineyards, that the Moraza family built its winery six generations ago. The family has been growing grapes and making wines since their beginning, and today it is run by the charismatic winemaker Janire Moraza.
Janire started getting involved in the late 2000s and her first vintage was 2013. With the help of her husband, Patricio Brongo, she formalized many of the ideas and practices that the family already applied to their farming - working without herbicides and chemicals, following a lunar cycle for pruning and racking - and started the process of biodynamic certification (the vineyards had been certified organic since 2006.) She tells us that when she started talking about biodynamics to her father, he told her that they were already using many of the principles. She improved on those and started making the 500 and 501 preparations to treat the vineyards, and a lot of work became focused on soils.
Today all of their 23 hectares have organic and biodynamic certifications. The majority of the parcels is found in San Vicente de la Sonsierra, but a couple are closer to Abalos, and Pecina, a little further along and north from the river. There is also one plot in La Bastid.  
In the cellar the work is minimal, and slightly atypical for Rioja in that none of the wines are made or staged in oak. As they make clear "our winery was completely built in concrete in 1983 according to the wine-making principles that prevailed in our ancestral house. It has been designed to work with gravity over three floors, so we can avoid over pumping and unnecessary manipulation. Loyal towards our philosophy of letting the fruit fully express itself, fermentation takes place spontaneously in concrete tanks with indigenous yeasts."  
The focus on purity of fruit is evident on all wines, which are bright and fresh on the palate, and enhance the character of each varietal. They work mostly with Viura for their whites and skin contact wine, but also make a Tempranillo Blanco and cultivate and use other native whites such as Calagrano. The reds are made of Tempranillo and are sometimes blended with Garnacha, and Graciano, which also shine singularly with a couple of monovarietal bottlings.  
Janire and her work is an excellent addition to our portfolio, and Bodegas Moraza is proof of the wide-range of wines and diverse character of Rioja, which we continue to explore and support at Bowler.Image:Region:
Description:
Since 1932, Bonnaire has been based in one of Champagne's finest crus, the village of Cramant, in the northern Côte des Blancs. In the wake of France’s financial crisis of 1929-30, founder Fernand Bouquement decided to stop selling his grapes to the houses and make his own champagne. This decision put him at the forefront of the grower champagne movement we now know. Fernand was joined by his son-in-law, André Bonnaire, after the Second World War. André proved to be passionate about vine growing and passed along his talents to his son, Jean-Louis, who elevated Bonnaire to one of the most renowned houses in the region. For the past decade, the winery has been run by brothers Jean-Emmanuel Bonnaire and Jean-Etienne Bonnaire, who took over for their father after 50 years of stewardship. Today, Champagne Bonnaire spans 13.5 hectares in Cramant, with additional holdings in Chouilly, Oiry, Bergeres les Vertus and Cuis.
While the winery was updated to a modern facility about 25 years ago, the approach to farming and winemaking remains rooted in the traditions passed down through generations. They are HVE certified and began the organic certification process in 2020. The brothers often harvest later than their neighbors, waiting for high levels of ripeness to provide roundness and minimize the need for dosage. Recently, they have been experimenting with grazing pigs, who offer a gentler alternative to mechanical weeding. In the cellar, vinification takes place in thermo-regulated stainless steel tanks and malolactic fermentation almost always occurs, softening the austerity that can result from the region’s chalky soils. The goal is a delectable tension between creamy and chiseled.
“The estate is known best for its creamy, opulent Blanc de Blancs. The vintage-dated Blanc de Blancs is pure Cramant, combining a concentrated ripeness with a racy, vibrant structure that makes it suitable for long aging” – Peter Liem, Champagne, 2017Image:Region:
Description:
The timbered home that houses this family-owned estate in Hainfeld was built in 1619, but the estate in its current form is far more recent than that. In 1990 Annette Borell and Thomas Diehl married and created Borell-Diehl by joining their families' three wineries into one. Starting with a total of 5 hectares, they have since expanded to 35 hectares of vineyards, all within 5km of Hainfeld, about 1/2 hour drive from Deidesheim. Their holdings are a complex geology of loess, limestone, red sandstone, with deposits of minerally
muschelkalk (limestone) in some sites.
Annette and Thomas' oldest son George has taken over leadership at the estate. Having staged at important addresses like Rebholz (Pfalz) Wittmann (Rheinhessen), and Von Volxem (Saar), as well as an internship in New Zealand in 2016, he continues the winery's focus on quality wines of extraordinary value. All the wines David Bowler imports are from estate-owned vineyards where rigorous crop thinning and hand-harvesting are the norm. In addition, no systemic pesticides or herbicides are used and there is no irrigation in the vineyards. As of 2018, the wines are certified vegan by the European Vegetarian Union.
Borell-Diehl is our cool, under-the-radar source for a slew of great wines "beyond Riesling," including:
\- fun, splashy liters of Müller-Thurgau and St. Laurent Rosé (our top-selling German wines!!!)
\- fabulous Gewürztraminer in a fruity Kabinett style
\- an excellent
methode champenoise Chardonnay Sekt
\- a classic Spätburgunder of such quality and value it would beat or compete with any American or French Pinot Noir under $20 that you'd care to name---a must try!

Established in 2002 by owner and winemaker Chris Brockway, Broc Cellars is a Berkeley-based winery focused on producing fresh, balanced California wines for everyday drinking. What began as a small négociant project has grown into a diverse range of more than 20 releases annually, sourced from organically farmed vineyards across the state. Broc emphasizes lesser-known varieties and site-driven expressions, rooted in transparency in both farming and winemaking.
An Omaha native, Chris worked in the restaurant world in Nebraska and the Pacific Northwest before eventually settling in California. As his interest in wine deepened, he enrolled in courses at UC Davis and later completed his degree in oenology at Fresno State, where he jokingly says he became an expert in everything he does not use. Through his early winemaking experiences with California Zinfandel, along with time spent at San Francisco’s first natural wine bars, Broc Cellars began to take shape as a move away from higher-alcohol, more extracted styles toward wines defined by energy, restraint, and drinkability.
From the outset, the approach has been intentionally minimal. Working exclusively with organically farmed fruit, fermentations are carried out with native yeasts, with no additions aside from a small amount of sulfur at bottling, depending on the wine, style, and vintage. Fruit is harvested to preserve natural acidity and at lower Brix levels for smoother fermentations and naturally lower alcohol, resulting in wines that feel lifted, vibrant, and balanced.
In recent years, Broc has evolved beyond its négociant origins. After more than a decade sourcing fruit from Fox Hill Vineyard in Mendocino, Brockway took over its farming in 2021 before purchasing the site in 2023. The 60-acre, CCOF-certified organic vineyard, planted largely to Italian varieties, marks a significant step toward estate farming, allowing for a deeper expression of the winery’s ethos while continuing to source from a diverse range of family-owned vineyards across California.

It's rare to find anyone in Chablis who farms biodynamically and it immediately drew my attention when the introduction to the Brocard wines crossed my desk. Even today, in 2023, there are only a handful of producers in Chablis practicing biodynamic viticulture. When Julien joined his father as vineyard manager in 1997 at Jean-Marc Brocard, the winery was using everything in the arsenal to combat disease: herbicides, fungicides, pesticides. Julien was determined that there had to be a better way. He had heard about biodynamic farming and became a part of a group of growers in Burgundy (which included Aubert de Villaine, Anne-Claude Leflaive and Dominique Lafon) who shared their trials and tribulations of farming this way. In 1997, he started his exploration with the village level “Boissoneuse” vineyard, which is the heart of the Julien Brocard winery.
Julien Brocard was the first to practice biodynamic farming in Chablis and it was not without its challenges. Growers from neighboring plots feared that biodynamic farming brought disease to their vineyards. Ignoring the naysayers and happy with the results, Julien pressed on and continued to convert more vineyards to biodynamic agriculture. In 2012, feeling that the sites were showing their fullest potential, he launched his own label, Julien Brocard - les 7 Lieux. “7 Lieux” translates to seven sites and he started with seven wines that year.  
Today, Julien is working with 18 hectares total, the heart of which is 11 hectares in the Boissoneuse vineyard in Préhy. Biodynamic farming requires constant human observation and attention, and the use of ancestral methods and tools, such as horse-drawn plowing which creates a natural link between people, the soil and the plants. Since planting fruit trees in the vineyard he has witnessed a resurgence of wildlife and microbial life in the soil. He’s working on the reforestation of his vineyards as well to help balance the water in the soil.Image:Region:
Description:
Brooklyn Cider House is owned and operated by Peter and Susan Yi. The story began in 2014 when Peter, former owner of PJ's Wine & Spirits in New York City, discovered the traditional ciders of Spain's Basque region during a wine trip. Until then, he had been a passionate wine lover with little interest in cider, but he returned from the trip a changed man.
Peter convinced his sister, Susan, to join him, and within a year they had purchased Twin Star Orchard in New Paltz, New York, which included 50 planted acres of mature heirloom apple varieties, along with additional younger plantings established after they took ownership. Their cider production began soon after, with their first releases arriving in the fall of 2015. Originally operating out of Bushwick, Brooklyn Cider House has since relocated its cidery to the orchard in the Hudson Valley.
In an effort to cultivate the highest-quality fruit for their ciders, the Yi family has incorporated organic and biodynamic farming practices, working toward a more sustainable and ecologically conscious operation. Today, Twin Star Orchard comprises roughly 100 acres planted to over 40 heirloom apple varieties, supplying fruit for the majority of their production. Additional fruit is sourced from nearby growers throughout the Hudson Valley.

Established in 1970 by the late Riccardo Bruna, Azienda Agricola Bruna is the benchmark producer of the local Pigato (AKA Vermentino\) grape, a late-ripening variety named for the amber spots that appear on the bunches. Located in the Arroscia valley in western Liguria, the historic home for Pigato, Bruna is a tiny 7.5 hectare estate consisting of 5-6 vineyard plots, all planted on terraced vineyards carved out of the mountainside. Production in a top year is only 3000 cases. The vineyards are perched at 200-300 meters above sea level and only 15km from the Mediterranean. This area, known as the Maritime Alps, is known for its production of olives, cherries and aromatic herbs, such as rosemary, thyme and sage. Bruna is run by Riccardo’s daughter Francesca and her husband, Roberto. The estate has worked organically (not certified) since 2009. In addition to its three Pigato wines, Bruna makes a Vermentino, a Rossese, and a two red blends based on the local
Granaccia variety, a variant of Grenache.
\“
Vermentino is actually Pigato. Wait a minute; no, Pigato is not Vermentino. After years debating the issue, researchers, wine experts and producers in Italy all agree to disagree on the subject. The academicians all apparently believe that Pigato and Vermentino are the same; many of Liguria’s wine producers do not. Being facetious, you might say that’s because the grapes are both Favorita. No, wait: they’re all Piccabon (a wrong attribution: we now know Piccabon is identical to Vernaccia di San Gimignano). And so the story goes on. And on

top of page
WINES FROM FAMILIES WORTH KNOWING
Wine exists to make you happier after opening the bottle than you were before. Everything else serves this goal.
Whether your happiness comes from a glass with friends at happy hour or a treasured bottle from the cellar, whether you relish the details of soil and site or just love the taste of wine, our job is to be your partner in that happiness.
Over two decades, we've found the most compelling wines come from producers who strive to create something exceptional from their corner of the world. These wines are full of life and character - from a rescued red grape variety in an unknown Loire appellation to a young woman fighting to preserve California's oldest vines. These are the wines we write home about.
The people making wines that reflect a unique site are usually the same folks working to preserve the environment that created such special wine. We wouldn't tell their stories if they weren't.
If a wine lands in Illinois with "Imported by Candid Wines" on the back label, we hope you find as much pleasure in the bottle as we found in bringing it to you.
About Us
MEET LOUIS CHENU PÉRE ET FILLES
Juliette and Caroline Chenu manage their family-run winery in the heart of Savigny-lès-Beaune. Founded in 1914 and led by two sisters, Louis Chenu Pere et Filles is a benchmark in the region. Located just minutes from the most well known sites in all of Burgundy, these Premiere Cru Pinot Noir represent stunning value.

Charles Neal
Charles Neal is an importer and distributor of wines and spirits based in San Francisco, California. His company, Charles Neal Selections, has been in existence since 1998. He is a leading authority on Armagnac and Calvados, having written benchmark books on both brandies, and increasingly so on Cognac as well. In addition to these spirits, Charles imports wonderful wines from nearly every French wine region, including numerous wines from Southwestern France, Bordeaux, the Loire Valley, Burgundy, Champagne, Jura, Beaujolais, Burgundy, the Northern Rhone, Southern Rhone, Bugey, Savoie and, most recently, the Lorraine and Corsica.
​
Spending a lot of time on airplanes, Charles travels to France five or six times a year and distributes wines and spirits in 17 states. While intimate with just about every wine making region in the country, he doesn’t know much about Paris as he’s normally too busy getting to his first appointments a few hours after arriving at CDG and talking too long at his last appointment before making his way back to the capital the night before leaving. For the past eighteen years he has navigated the back roads of France, tirelessly attempting to find wine growers from areas often neglected by other importers. His philosophy remains rather simple: find high quality wines from small growers that display the grape variety from which they come and the terroir upon which they are grown while getting them to a customer at a fair price.
In pursuit of this philosophy, Charles has sought out and brought attention to wines from relatively unknown appellations like Madiran, Jurançon, Gaillac, Fronton, Marcillac and Béarn, as well as the unheralded Alpine crus of Chignin, Arbin, Apremont, Ripaille and Marestel. He has also cultivated a small but highly regarded grower champagne portfolio, becoming one of the greatest supporters of these small growers in their effort to challenge the old behemoth Champagne houses.
​

For the past eighteen years he has navigated the back roads of France, tirelessly attempting to find wine growers from areas often neglected by other importers. His philosophy remains rather simple: find high quality wines from small growers that display the grape variety from which they come and the terroir upon which they are grown while getting them to a customer at a fair price.
In pursuit of this philosophy, Charles has sought out and brought attention to wines from relatively unknown appellations like Madiran, Jurançon, Gaillac, Fronton, Marcillac and Béarn, as well as the unheralded Alpine crus of Chignin, Arbin, Apremont, Ripaille and Marestel. He has also cultivated a small but highly regarded grower champagne portfolio, becoming one of the greatest supporters of these small growers in their effort to challenge the old behemoth Champagne houses.
Picture Charles himself puts it best:
Obviously it’s easier to talk about a band, chef, writer or filmmaker when they easily fit into one specific category. “He writes noir fiction.” “They’re a metal band.” “She’s an Italian chef.” “He makes violent movies.” We like to do this with wine importers too: “They deal with German wines.” They sell natural wines.” “They have California boutique wines.” “Their focus is Italian wines.” Or, “All of their wines are organic.”
It’s great to be known for something, in that you’ve made some progress in enlightening people to a certain type of wine. But that doesn’t mean that that category is all that you do. It is difficult to generalize or pigeonhole much of what Charles Neal Selections does. We work with a great deal of producers from the Southwest but those producers comprise only about 15% of CNS sales. The company actually sells much more Champagne, Burgundy or Loire Valley wine than wine from the great Southwest. We ask that people not ignore areas like the Jura, Savoie or Bugey, but we thoroughly understand that there is a bigger market for producers from more well-known regions, so we choose them with the same care and patience as those from smaller, less-known regions.
We could say that most of our producers are small. But we are beginning to dislike the word small when talking about production because smaller production alone doesn’t always mean better production. Small production often means amateur production. But small is also a relative word; what is small anyway? 3 million cases as opposed to 10 million? 6,000 as opposed to 15,000? 1,200 as opposed to 5,000? The producers imported by Charles Neal Selections average 6,000 cases (that is 72,000 bottles) of wine per year. This normally means that the producers have somewhere between 10 and 20 hectares of vines with their winery nearby.
We work with family owned wineries throughout France. But this is another phrase that can easily be spun. Just who is family? Are they a dysfunctional bourgeois clan that hires an enologist and treats their employees with little respect? Are they a negoçiant firm owned by a family but who buys most of their grapes and are not involved with the winemaking? Or are they a family that actually gets their hands and shoes dirty in the vineyards and lives in a modest home on the property?
95% of the producers in the CNS Catalogue fall into this final category--humble producers carrying on a tradition from generations past and building a future for generations to come. We love spending time with our producers and eating and drinking with them in their homes. We love having discussions, getting in arguments, laughing and shooting the shit, often until midnight or after. It’s great to have visited or stayed at a domaine for more than a decade and watch a producer’s kids grow up around you. Many of them have seen our kids grow up too. One day they’re riding a bicycle, then a road bike, then a motorcycle.
We prefer to see wine producers at their domaines, rather than encountering them at wine trade fairs like Vin Expo, Vini Sud, the Loire Valley Wine Fair or Millisime Bio. While that is not a bad place to do one stop shopping and is par for the course for many importers and distributors, it’s just not our bag: those environs always seem so artificial, kind of like a wine shopping mall. We like seeing producers on their properties, so that we can get to know them over lunch, see how they work their vines, and observe the state of their cellars.
Most of our producers are well respected in their native regions, and are well-known, liked and respected by other growers in other appellations. We’re proud of the fact that these producers have continued to hone their craft, reintroducing techniques in their vineyards or upgrading equipment in their cellars to ultimately produce better wines.
That doesn’t mean that certain producers are not capable of putting out some crowd-pleasing wines in relatively large quantities; we like nothing more than to supply our distributors with wines that they can place by the glass or sell repeatedly to retailers. We now have a hard time keeping some of these in stock but are working hard to have a steady pipeline of core wines that nevertheless display the fruit of their grapes and minerality of their terroir.
We have never been reliant on the press to help sell our wines. Our wines do get reviewed frequently, but we have never thrown down press with distributors, stores or restaurants. We understand that this is the policy of many other importers, yet we’ve always felt that the people that buy our wine buy more based on their own palates and knowledge of their customers rather than on scores.
​
.
By law, Charles Neal Selections can only import and distribute wines and spirits to licensed wholesalers, retail stores and restaurants

results.title: Westwood Estate | Biodynamic and Organic Farming
results.content:
Today, we are one of a handful of Demeter-certified Biodynamic vineyards in North America. Why don’t more people do it? It’s expensive. Between the physical workload and lower yields from the vines, costs can be 50%-100% greater than with conventional farming. However, it is catching on fast! Virtually all Grand Cru Burgundy producers farm Biodynamically and are being closely followed by the top-tier producers in Bordeaux and around the world.

An unexpected gem of a vineyard on the northern edge of the Sonoma Valley that we discovered over twenty years ago. And we have a very special place in the Sonoma Valley’s Annadel Gap – thirty-three unique acres.
We farm Biodynamically and Organically.
We farm Biodynamically and Organically. [...] After a painstaking multi-year process, we were awarded Demeter Biodynamic certification in 2016 and CCOF Organic certification in 2017. Every grape grown on our Annadel Gap Estate is certified Demeter Biodynamic and CCOF Organic – carefully tended with the most eco-responsible methods available.
results.rawContent:
Westwood Estate WineryWestwood Estate Winery

A Certified Biodynamic and Organic Vineyard. Sustainability is at the core of our soil and our soul.
Every wine we make begins with Biodynamic, Organic, and Sustainable fruit. Sustaining the land, animals, and the team that makes our wine possible is the foundation of our culture. It’s the “How” to the question of “How we make Unforgettable Wines.” You see it in the way we treat each other, our supplier-partners, our fellow farmer-winemakers, and our community. And you see it in the way we treat our lands.
We believe these farming practices not only enhance the health of the land but also allow us to create natural wines that are pure expressions of their home. Wines of character come from soils with healthy biomes that form a balanced ecosystem with the vine and nourish it with flavors most natural to the vineyard.
Our mission to create unforgettable wines begins right here on our home vineyard, the Annadel Gap Vineyard. An unexpected gem of a vineyard on the northern edge of the Sonoma Valley that we discovered over twenty years ago. And we have a very special place in the Sonoma Valley’s Annadel Gap – thirty-three unique acres.
We farm Biodynamically and Organically.
We farm Biodynamically and Organically.
After a painstaking multi-year process, we were awarded Demeter Biodynamic certification in 2016 and CCOF Organic certification in 2017. Every grape grown on our Annadel Gap Estate is certified Demeter Biodynamic and CCOF Organic – carefully tended with the most eco-responsible methods available.
Biodynamics is the highest level of organic farming – Organic squared! Developed in the 1920s by Dr. Rudolf Steiner, Biodynamics treats the vineyard as a single living organism. Eliminating synthetic fertilizers and pesticides is the beginning, but Biodynamics goes further, encouraging extreme biodiversity, a closed nutrient system, the use of natural “teas” and a personal connection to the land. In harmony with the lunar cycle, Steiner believed this discipline results in a self-sustaining cycle of living and higher energy to the fruit.
Since our transition to Biodynamics, our vines have become stronger, more disease-resistant, and the roots have deepened dramatically – now requiring virtually no irrigation. Our vineyard is healthy and balanced, and wildlife – jackrabbits and toads especially – are super-abundant. And we swear, you can sense the higher energy in the place and the wines!
Today, we are one of a handful of Demeter-certified Biodynamic vineyards in North America. Why don’t more people do it? It’s expensive. Between the physical workload and lower yields from the vines, costs can be 50%-100% greater than with conventional farming. However, it is catching on fast! Virtually all Grand Cru Burgundy producers farm Biodynamically and are being closely followed by the top-tier producers in Bordeaux and around the world.
Cared for by a Biodynamic legend.
Cared for by a Biodynamic legend.
Philippe Coderey is a legend in the natural, Organic, and Biodynamic viticulture field. Philippe serves as our Biodynamic Vineyard Consultant, leading the viticulture team to implement the Biodynamic and Organic practices across the whole vineyard. Philippe’s last name comes from the French verb, “couderer,” which means to cultivate vineyards. He grew up on vineyards in Provençe, learning traditional and natural viticultural techniques from elders. He puts all of his passion and knowledge to work in our vineyards.
We are partners with our land.
We believe we are stewards of the land. It’s only ours for a little while, and then it is someone else’s honor to tend to it. We are pesticide-free and herbicide-free. We follow the cycles of nature (check out our calendar below), sowing cover crops to protect the soil and attract beneficial bugs. Our hand-crafted wines begin right here in the vineyard, with our hand-made, nutrient-dense Biodynamic sprays and organic composts, all applied by hand.

Our rewards are many.
Our rewards are many.
We are rewarded with prospering vines and a variety of wildlife calling our estate their home. We are rewarded by the health of labor and the richness of being close to the earth. And we are rewarded with grapes that make opulent, distinctive, and unforgettable wines.

results.content:
Respect for the vineyards is a cornerstone principle of Bronco Wine Co. and a commitment to sustainability and environmental responsibility runs through every aspect of our enterprise.
Quality
Bronco Wine Co. shares an unwavering commitment to growing, producing, and selling the finest quality wines of the highest value to our diverse customers worldwide.
Heritage Brands [...] Our Values
As a family-owned company, we strive to continue and improve upon being vertically integrated, from the vineyard to the table, focusing on crafting quality wines for every table. Our family’s resilience and sustained growth will continue to be fostered through stewardship of family, valued employees, respected partners, and future generations.
Environmental Responsibility [...] Heritage Brands
Bronco Wine Co. has a vast portfolio of brands from multiple appellations across the western United States, Europe, and South America.
Family History
results.rawContent:
Our Values
As a family-owned company, we strive to continue and improve upon being vertically integrated, from the vineyard to the table, focusing on crafting quality wines for every table. Our family’s resilience and sustained growth will continue to be fostered through stewardship of family, valued employees, respected partners, and future generations.
Environmental Responsibility
Respect for the vineyards is a cornerstone principle of Bronco Wine Co. and a commitment to sustainability and environmental responsibility runs through every aspect of our enterprise.
Quality
Bronco Wine Co. shares an unwavering commitment to growing, producing, and selling the finest quality wines of the highest value to our diverse customers worldwide.
Heritage Brands
Bronco Wine Co. has a vast portfolio of brands from multiple appellations across the western United States, Europe, and South America.
Family History
December 27, 2023, marked the 50th anniversary of Bronco Wine Co. and since its inception, it has remained family-owned. For the past half-century, Bronco Wine Co. has been at the forefront of innovation, disruption, and sustainability in the wine category, creating high-quality wines that over-deliver across price points and will continue to do so for generations to come.
